title: Steady rollout kinematics — warmup timelines, KPIs, and rollback heuristics (personal notes)
content:
Context and purpose:
This is a compact, personal reference for small-to-medium model flips and model-config changes where we want predictable user impact and fast escape hatches. I call it 'kinematics' because I want an intuition around velocity (rate of traffic change) and acceleration (how quickly we change that rate).

Assumptions:
- Target users: internal canaries + progressively larger client cohorts.
- Baseline telemetry available: p50/p95 latency, errors per 1k reqs, tokens/sec per GPU, model-quality scoring (eval hooks on small prompt sets), cache hit ratio, KV-cache warmup time.
- We can pin at tenant-level and have per-tenant backoff flags.

Goals:
- Minimal user-visible blips (latency or error noise) during warmup.
- Avoid expensive gamma (sudden) traffic moves that cause long tail latencies.
- Provide a single-person actionable checklist for roll-forward / rollback within first 20 minutes.

Key terms (my shorthand):
- velocity: fraction points of total traffic moved per minute (e.g., 0.5%/min).
- momentum: current moving avg of velocity over last 5 min (used to gate next step).
- heat-check: 90s window sampling of latency, errors, and model-quality spike tests.
- warm cohort: small user subset used to pre-warm KV/cache and exercise common prompts.

Example ramp profile (conservative):
- Step 0 (priming): 0% -> 0.2% traffic for 3 min. Purpose: warm caches, confirm startup memory/ooms.
- Step 1 (micro canary): 0.2% -> 1% over 10 min (velocity ~0.08%/min). Heat-check at t+3m and t+8m.
- Step 2 (small cohort): 1% -> 5% over 20 min (velocity ~0.2%/min). Heat-check every 5m.
- Step 3 (medium cohort): 5% -> 20% over 40 min (velocity ~0.375%/min). Heat-checks and run the 50-sample eval set every 10m.
- Step 4 (wide): 20% -> 60% over 60 min. If no regression, move to full after 90–120m observation.
Notes: these numbers are intentionally slow for stateful inference where KV cache matters. For stateless small requests you can accelerate (2x) after a successful Step 1.

Ramp gating heuristics (quick checks before increasing to next step):
- Latency: p95 <= baseline_p95 * 1.6 OR absolute p95 < baseline_p95 + 200ms (whichever stricter).
- Errors: error_rate < baseline_error_rate + 0.5% AND no new 5xx patterns.
- Resource signals: GPU mem pressure < 85%, queue depth stable (no >2x jump), token/sec within 10% of expected for the cohort.
- Quality: model-quality score on the 50-sample eval set has delta >= -1% (no serious regressions).
- Momentum check: average velocity in last 5m must be <= planned velocity * 1.2 (prevents runaway accelerations).

Immediate rollback triggers (manual immediate rollback):
- p95 > baseline_p95 * 2 sustained for 90s.
- Error rate spike > 2% absolute for 60s.
- OOMs or repeated infra restarts for the model process.
- Quality regression: specific golden prompt failures where output is empty, truncated, or hallucinating sensitive content (flagged by eval hooks).

Soft rollback (stepwise backoff) rules:
- If minor breach (latency/p95 ~1.6–2x baseline or error increase 0.5–2%), reduce to previous step and hold for 15–30m, increase sampling of golden prompts, and escalate if no recovery.
- If infra signal (mem pressure) present, divert new traffic to fallback model variant (e.g., smaller quantized model) and set emergency pin for affected tenants.

Quick CLI commands I keep in my head:
- Flip cohort to model-X: redwoodctl rollout set --model model-X --cohort <cohort-id> --fraction 0.01
- Warm cohort: redwoodctl rollout set --warm true --cohort <id>
- Pin tenant to old: redwoodctl tenant pin --tenant <t> --model <old-model>
- Force rollback: redwoodctl rollout abort --rollout-id <id> --reason "latency spike"
(These are pseudo-CLI; check the exact flags in the console.)

Telemetry and dashboards to watch (high-priority):
- p50/p95/p99 latency (global + by-region + by-tenant)
- 5xx/4xx counts and error-class fingerprints (stack traces)
- per-model token/sec and avg sequence length in the cohort
- cache hit ratio and KV-cache warmup curve for warm cohort
- small eval-set quality score trend and diff table
- per-instance GPU memory headroom and queued request counts

Priming cohort design (practical notes):
- Use a combination of: internal nightly traffic replay (~2k requests/min with realistic seq lengths), 10–20 real clients opted-in, and synthetic prompt bank covering heavy-tail prompts.
- Run a quick 'golden prompt' set (10 prompts) every 5m during Steps 1–3, lower cadence after Step 4.

Post-rollout checks (first 24h):
- 0–2h: minute-level checks for latency and errors; make sure cache hit ratio stabilizes.
- 2–6h: hourly quality checks on a larger eval set (200 samples).
- 6–24h: daily cohort sampling for edge-case prompts, confirm no slow regressions.

Experiment ideas (things to try):
- Momentum-aware ramp: dynamically adjust velocity based on a momentum metric that dampens increases when velocity is high but no stability signal.
- Cache pre-warm windows tied to client timezone: schedule slow priming for regions before business hours.
- Adaptive cohort sizing: if the model-quality delta is favorable and infra signals are better-than-baseline, accelerate by a multiplier (1.5x) automatically with guardrails.

Open questions / unknowns (to resolve before next big flip):
- How to best surface model-quality regression root cause (prompt-level vs model-level) in the rollout console quickly?
- Can we automate a two-minute micro-rollback that only affects newly arrived requests (keep in-flight unaffected)?
- Should momentum use p50 or p95-based velocity? My instinct is p95 for safety but p50 is more stable for noisy workloads.

Personal checklist before I touch traffic (my habit):
[ ] Confirm baseline windows (last 24h) and capture snapshots.
[ ] Notify on-call + SRE slack channel with planned timeline and escape hatch.
[ ] Start priming cohort and wait for 3 min warm window.
[ ] Validate golden prompts pass 3 consecutive checks.
[ ] Move to Step 1 velocity target and set heat-check timers.
[ ] Keep terminal handy; pre-fill rollback command.

End notes (less formal):
- I like slow, observable moves for anything stateful. The math of cache warmup means a lot of sudden ramps look worse than they are because you pay cache-miss costs early. Slower ramps let cache hit ratios amortize.
- If you only remember one rule: avoid >2x p95 jumps for longer than 90s without reverting. Everything else is negotiable.

Timestamp of last edit: 2026-03-10 — quick tidy after a noisy flip that went well (notes above updated).

Scratch margin: experiments I want to run next week:
- Run a 4-step auto momentum policy in staging and capture the 'time to stable p95' vs manual ramp.
- Build a tiny dashboard card that shows velocity + momentum + last heat-check outcome in a single line.
